nameStory: The "proliferous" in this pink's name comes from Latin meaning "bearing offspring," referring to how the plant produces clusters of small flowers that seem to multiply from papery bracts. It belongs to the pink family, named for the fringed or "pinked" edges of many species' petals, like fabric cut with pinking shears.
description: Proliferous Pink is a small, delicate annual herb that grows 4-12 inches tall with thin, wiry stems. This European native produces tiny pink flowers clustered together within distinctive papery, silvery bracts that look almost like little lanterns. The plant has narrow, grass-like leaves and an overall fine, wispy appearance that can easily be overlooked among other vegetation.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink flowers (about 1/8 inch across) emerge from distinctive papery, silvery-white bracts that feel dry and crinkly to the touch, like tissue paper

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, linear leaves that feel smooth and are arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, resembling thin grass blades

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual with thin, wiry stems that branch from the base, creating a small tuft rarely taller than your hand

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small capsules develop within the papery bracts, splitting to release tiny dark seeds

habitat: Look for Proliferous Pink in disturbed sandy or gravelly soils, particularly along roadsides, in waste places, or on rocky slopes. It prefers well-drained, poor soils and full sun, typical of many European weeds that have found footholds in similar habitats across New England.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants develop their characteristic narrow leaves in a small basal tuft.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from June through August, when the distinctive papery bracts and tiny pink flowers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to dry out and turn brown, with seeds maturing and dispersing from the papery capsules.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil.

funFact: Despite being recorded only once in New England, this tiny immigrant has managed to spread across much of North America by hitching rides in soil, gravel, and construction materials - its papery seed cases are perfectly designed to catch the wind and tumble along roads like miniature tumbleweeds.
confusionNotes: The papery, silvery bracts immediately distinguish this from other small pink flowers. Without flowers, the grass-like leaves might be confused with young grasses, but the opposite leaf arrangement (grasses have alternate leaves) is the key difference.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, making it more of a botanical curiosity than a plant most nature explorers will encounter. It's much more common in the western United States where it has become well-established.
compareHints: Proliferous Pink differs from its relative Tunicflower by having flowers clustered tightly within prominent papery bracts, while Tunicflower has more open flower clusters. Both share the narrow leaves and small pink flowers, but the "paper lantern" bracts of Proliferous Pink are unmistakable when present.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tunicflower can be distinguished from its relative Proliferous Pink by its solitary flowers at branch tips, while Proliferous Pink has clusters of flowers bunched together.
